title: Wide-field calcium imaging of cortex-wide activity in awake, head-fixed mice
protocol: Anesthetize the adult mouse with isoflurane in an induction box.
Transfer the anesthetized mouse to an isoflurane ventilator with a nose cone.
Regulate the percent isoflurane to achieve steady breathing rates throughout surgery.
Maintain body temperature using a servo-controlled heating pad during surgery.
Cover the eyes with copious amounts of Vaseline to protect against drying and irritant chemicals.
Clean and antisepticize the surgical region.
Make a small incision (∼2 mm) on the scalp using fine scissors.
Make a small incision in the scalp.
Cut out a circular piece of scalp to expose the skull covering the dorsal cortex and cerebellum.
Remove the periosteum gently from the skull surface using a scalpel.
Detach muscles from the occipital bone within the black dashed line area with a scalpel.
Insert gel foam pieces into gaps between detached muscles and the occipital bone to stop bleeding.
Wipe the skull thoroughly with cotton swabs soaked in 3% hydrogen peroxide to remove any soft tissues.
Dry the skull completely before proceeding further.
Apply small drops of cyanoacrylate glue over the muscles and occipital bone area marked by the black dashed line.
Allow the cyanoacrylate glue to cure.
Add dental acrylic cement using a double-end carver to build a thick layer on top of the cured cyanoacrylate glue.
Cover skin along the cuts with cyanoacrylate glue using a double-end carver.
Implant the headbar.
Apply a small amount of cyanoacrylate glue to the interparietal bone.
Place the headbar ∼0.5–1 mm posterior to the lambda.
Adjust the angle of the headbar until it is parallel to the transverse plane of the skull.
Hold the headbar in place until it stays steady.
Secure the headbar.
Add drops of cyanoacrylate glue to build a glue layer between the headbar and cement.
Let the glue cure.
Apply dental acrylic cement around the headbar to build up the attachment between bones and the headbar.
Make sure the bones posterior to the lambda and the middle part of the headbar are entirely covered.
Let the dental acrylic cement cure.
Build the cyanoacrylate glue layer on the skull.
Apply a small amount of cyanoacrylate glue and evenly distribute it to form a thin layer covering the entire skull.
Wait for the cyanoacrylate glue to cure to form a solid, smooth, and transparent layer.
Repeat 3–4 times to thicken the glue layer.
Protect the eyes from the excitation light of imaging.
Cut a chunk (∼5 mm) of black heat shrink tube (∼2 cm diameter).
Glue the cut heat shrink tube to the circumference of the skull using cyanoacrylate glue.
Fill the gap between the heat shrink tube and mouse head with black dental acrylic cement from the outside.
Clean and antisepticize the scalp and the surrounding region.
Wipe the surgical region with cotton swabs soaked in 70% ethanol 2–3 times.
Wipe the surgical region with cotton swabs soaked in betadine until the entire surgical region has been infiltrated.
Make a small incision (∼2 mm) on the scalp between two ears using fine scissors.
Starting from the small incision, cut off a circular piece of the scalp to expose the skull covering the dorsal cortex and cerebellum.
Retract the remaining scalp around the cuts with forceps to fully expose the dorsal skull.
Use forceps to lift the scalp near the eyes.
Confirm the location of the retro-orbital sinus before proceeding.
Remove the periosteum on the skull surface gently with a scalpel.
Press the bleeding spot with a dry cotton swab if bone bleeding occurs until it stops.
Rinse the skull with saline to remove bloodstains after removing the periosteum.
Clean along the bone sutures carefully to avoid bleeding under the skull.
Detach muscles from the occipital bone with a scalpel.
Push detached muscles away to extend the bone interface for glue and cement application.
Insert small pieces of gel foam into gaps between muscles and the occipital bone to stop bleeding.
Moisten gel foam with saline if necessary.
Check the skull to ensure it is clean and smooth.
Detach muscles gently to avoid damaging the occipital bone and skull surface.
Press on bleeding sites with clean, dry cotton swabs if bleeding is heavy.
Rinse the skull with saline if blood spreads to the skull surface.
Wipe the skull with dry cotton swabs after stopping bleeding to remove bloodstains.
Terminate surgery and exclude the animal from the experiment if bleeding continues for more than 20 minutes.
Soak cotton swabs in 3% hydrogen peroxide and use them to wipe the skull to remove soft tissues.
Wait approximately 5 minutes for the dorsal skull to dry.
Monitor that the skull becomes whiter and less transparent as it dries.
Ensure the skull is dry before proceeding with cyanoacrylate glue application.
If necessary, use a compressed air duster gently to facilitate drying of the skull.
Remove gel foam between muscles and the occipital bone using forceps.
Apply small drops of cyanoacrylate glue to cover the muscles and the occipital bone.
After curing, apply dental acrylic cement with a double-end carver on top of the glue layer.
Use cyanoacrylate glue to cover the skin along the cuts.
Apply a small amount of cyanoacrylate glue to the interparietal bone for headbar attachment.
Adjust the angle of the headbar until it is parallel to the transverse plane of the skull.
Hold the headbar in place until it stays steady.
Add drops of cyanoacrylate glue through the holes on the headbar to build a glue layer between the headbar and cement.
Apply dental acrylic cement around the headbar to build up the attachment between bones and the headbar.
Ensure that the bones posterior to the lambda are entirely covered with dental acrylic cement.
Embed the middle part of the headbar in cement to secure it further.
Let the dental acrylic cement cure.
Build a thin cyanoacrylate glue layer on the skull.
Apply a small amount of cyanoacrylate glue to the skull over the dorsal cortex.
Evenly distribute the glue using a double-end carver to cover the entire skull.
Wait for the cyanoacrylate glue to cure to form a solid, smooth, and transparent layer.
Repeat the step 3-4 times.
Blow off debris with a compressed air duster if necessary.
Reapply cyanoacrylate glue to form a smooth and transparent layer after drilling off any excess glue or dealing with bleeding.
Cut a chunk (∼5 mm) of black heat shrink tube (∼2 cm diameter).
Glue the cut chunk around the circumference of the skull using cyanoacrylate glue.
Fill the gap between the heat shrink tube and mouse head with black dental acrylic cement from the outside.
Cover the cured cement layer with a layer of black electrical tape or paint it with black marker pens to block light.
Ensure that the black dental acrylic cement does not flow onto the transparent glue layer on the dorsal skull.
Avoid retinal damage by minimizing exposure to excitation blue light (∼485 nm) during imaging.
Inject Buprenorphine subcutaneously at a dose of 0.1 mg/kg for pain relief.
Inject Baytril subcutaneously at a dose of 10 mg/kg to prevent infection.
Monitor the mouse as it recovers from anesthesia after dental acrylic cement has cured.
Check the optical clarity of the skull-intact preparation frequently post-surgery.

If the preparation appears cloudy and yellow, indicating potential infection, inject a mixture of Baytril (10 mg/kg) and Dexamethasone (1 mg/kg) subcutaneously for 3-5 consecutive days to treat infection and reduce inflammation.
Terminate the experiment if continued infection or lack of clarity persists in the skull preparation.
Prepare the imaging setup.
Turn on the imaging light source (HXP 200 C, Zeiss).
Turn on the microscope (Axio Zoom.V16 equipped with an objective lens (1 ×, 0.25 NA, FWD 56 mm), Zeiss).
Turn on the camera (ORCA-Flash4.0, Hamamatsu).
Open the HCImage Live software (Hamamatsu).
Set frame size to 512 × 512 pixels.
Set frame rate to 30 Hz.
Fix the mouse to the stage under the microscope through the headbar.
Clean the window surface with cotton swabs soaked in 70% ethanol.
Choose the field of view (FOV).
Adjust the position of the stage to place the cortex in the center of the FOV (∼11 mm × 11 mm).
Adjust the height of the objective until the blood vessels are in focus.
Minimize the power of excitation light during imaging to avoid photobleaching of GCaMP signals.
Adjust the power of the excitation light to 10–20 mW for imaging GCaMP6s in cortical excitatory neurons.
Ensure the brightest pixels are around 50–60% of the full dynamic range.
Use the average frame from the first imaging session as a reference image.
Align the field of view based on landmarks visible in the reference image during repeated imaging sessions.
Adjust the position of the stage to align the x–y location with landmarks.
Adjust the height of the objective until blood vessels show similar clarity as the reference image.
